title: HUSBANDS, LOVE YOUR WIVES: THE COMMAND THAT EXPOSES WHAT KIND OF MAN YOU REALLY ARE
paragraphs: HUSBANDS, LOVE YOUR WIVES: THE COMMAND THAT EXPOSES WHAT KIND OF MAN YOU REALLY ARE
God Never Commanded You to Be Her King. He Commanded You to Love Her Like Christ Loved the Church. And That Changes Everything.
What if the greatest failure in your marriage isn't that you've stopped providing for your wife… but that you've stopped loving her the way Jesus commanded?
You pay the bills. You work until your body aches. You make sure there's food on the table, electricity in the house, and a roof over your family's head.
And somewhere along the way, you began believing that should be enough.
But one evening, your wife sits quietly beside you.
She's not arguing. She's not complaining. She's not even asking you for anything.
She's just… quiet.
You assume everything is fine.
What you don't realize is that she has spent months learning how to live with a loneliness she never expected to experience while married.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part?
She's lying beside the very man who promised she would never have to face life alone.
Brother, this isn't written to humiliate you.

It's written because there is a command in Scripture that we have read so many times, quoted so confidently, and sometimes obeyed so poorly that we've forgotten how terrifyingly beautiful it actually is.
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." — Ephesians 5:25 (KJV)
Read those last words again.
Gave Himself for it.
Not merely His money.
Not merely His spare time.
Not merely the leftovers of His energy after everything else had received His attention.
Himself.
And if we understand what Paul was actually saying, this single verse has the power to dismantle generations of pride, selfishness, emotional neglect, and distorted ideas of biblical manhood.
Because God did not tell husbands to love their wives according to what their wives deserve.
He told them to look at Jesus.
And that is a standard no man can meet through pride or human strength alone.
The original Greek of Ephesians 5:25 begins:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas.
Literally: "Husbands, love your wives."
The word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) is a present imperative, a command expressed in a form that naturally calls for ongoing action.
Paul isn't describing an occasional romantic gesture.
He is commanding a way of life.
Not simply, "Love her when she makes you happy."
Not, "Love her when she respects your decisions."
Not, "Love her when the house is peaceful and your needs are satisfied."
Love her.
Continually.
Faithfully.
Deliberately.
And then Paul makes the command almost unbearably weighty:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς
K athōs kai ho Christos ēgapēsen tēn ekklēsian kai heauton paredōken hyper autēs.
"Just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself up for her."
The crucial word is παρέδωκεν (paredōken), from paradidōmi, meaning to hand over or give up.
Paul is pointing us toward the self-giving sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
The cross.
The place where love became visible through suffering.
The place where the innocent Savior willingly gave Himself for sinners.
And suddenly the question is no longer, "Does my wife appreciate everything I do?"
The question becomes:
"Does the way I treat my wife resemble the Savior who gave Himself for me?"
That question should make every husband examine his heart.
Because some men want the authority associated with being a husband while resisting the sacrifice commanded of a husband.
They want their voices respected but refuse to listen.
They want forgiveness but struggle to apologize.
They expect patience when they fail but become harsh when their wives make mistakes.
They quote Scripture about submission while conveniently overlooking the verse commanding them to lay down their own selfishness.
But brother, you cannot use the Bible to demand honor while refusing the Bible's command to love.
And you cannot claim to represent Christ in your marriage while using fear, humiliation, or intimidation to control the woman entrusted to your care.
Jesus did not establish His kingdom through domestic tyranny.
He washed feet.
He welcomed the weary.
He spoke truth.
He confronted sin.
He gave Himself.
And the more closely a husband follows Christ, the less comfortable he should become with selfishness disguised as leadership.
Remember what happened in John 13.
Jesus knew who He was.
He knew the Father had given all things into His hands.
He knew where He had come from and where He was going.
And with that knowledge of His authority, He took a towel and washed His disciples' feet.
Think about that.
The One with all authority chose the posture of a servant.
So why do some husbands imagine that spiritual leadership means they are too important to serve?
Why should a man feel diminished by washing dishes, caring for children, listening patiently, or helping his exhausted wife when the Lord of glory stooped to wash feet?
A man does not become less masculine by serving his wife. He becomes more like Jesus.
And that is where this command begins to hurt.
Because love is relatively easy to discuss when everyone is smiling.
It's harder when your wife is frustrated.
When the finances are tight.
When intimacy has become complicated.
When children are demanding.
When the house is noisy.
When both of you are exhausted and neither feels understood.
It is in those moments that your theology stops being something you quote and becomes something you practice.
Colossians 3:19 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them." (KJV)
The Greek expression translated "be not bitter" uses πικραίνεσθε (pikrainesthe), a verb associated with becoming bitter or embittered.
Paul prohibits husbands from allowing bitterness to shape their treatment of their wives.
And bitterness does not always announce itself through shouting.
Sometimes it sounds like sarcasm.
Sometimes it looks like constant criticism.
Sometimes it becomes deliberate emotional distance.
Sometimes it appears as a husband who refuses to speak for days because he knows silence will punish his wife more effectively than an argument.
Sometimes it's the cutting remark disguised as a joke.
And sometimes it's the frightening moment when a woman realizes she must carefully manage her husband's moods to feel safe in her own home.
Brother, that is not Christlike love.
A wife should not have to earn freedom from cruelty by becoming perfectly agreeable.
Nor should a husband mistake his wife's silence for peace.
There are women who have stopped arguing because they feel hopeless about being heard.
There are wives who no longer share their fears because vulnerability has repeatedly been met with dismissal.
There are women who appear strong in public but privately wonder why the person closest to them seems least interested in their hearts.
And there are husbands reading this who never intended to become that man.
You didn't stand at the altar planning to grow cold.
You didn't exchange vows hoping that one day your wife would feel invisible.
Perhaps you watched unhealthy marriages growing up.
Perhaps nobody ever taught you how to express tenderness.
Perhaps your father provided financially but rarely apologized, embraced, listened, or said, "I love you."
Perhaps you learned to survive through emotional distance and carried that survival habit into marriage.
Those experiences may help explain your struggles.
But they do not make unloving behavior righteous.
And they do not mean your story must end this way.
Because Jesus Christ does more than forgive the past.
He transforms people who surrender their lives to Him.
The Gospel does not merely offer men a better marriage strategy.
It offers sinners a new heart.
And sometimes repentance begins with a sentence that feels almost impossible for a proud man to speak.
"I was wrong."
Not, "I'm sorry you feel that way."
Not, "I'm sorry, but you made me angry."
Not, "You know how much pressure I'm under."
Just…
"I was wrong. I hurt you. Please forgive me."
No excuses.
No shifting blame.
No demand that forgiveness arrive immediately.
And no expectation that one apology will erase years of pain.
Because biblical repentance is not simply feeling guilty after being confronted.
It is turning away from sin and bearing fruit consistent with that change.
A husband who has wounded his wife may need to rebuild trust slowly, through sustained humility, honesty, accountability, and changed behavior.

If there has been abuse, repentance includes ending the abuse, accepting consequences, and respecting his wife's need for safety and appropriate outside support. Scripture never requires a wife to remain in danger to prove her faithfulness.
Love does not demand that another person become unsafe so that your pride can remain untouched.
And if that sentence makes you uncomfortable, consider how Peter addressed husbands.
In 1 Peter 3:7, husbands are commanded to live with their wives according to knowledge, showing them honor as fellow heirs of the grace of life.
The original Greek includes the phrase:
συγκληρονόμοις χάριτος ζωῆς
Synklēronomois charitos zōēs.
"Fellow heirs of the grace of life."
Fellow heirs.
Not spiritually inferior possessions.
Not household servants.
Not people whose worth depends on how effectively they satisfy a husband's preferences.
Fellow heirs of God's gracious gift.
And Peter adds a sobering warning: husbands must honor their wives so that their prayers will not be hindered.
Imagine that.
A man may be deeply concerned about the appearance of his spiritual life while neglecting the person he vowed to cherish.
He may speak passionately about prayer while treating his wife dishonorably.
Peter refuses to separate a husband's relationship with God from his conduct toward his wife.
You cannot compartmentalize cruelty and call the rest of your life holiness.
And there is something else we need to confront.
Your wife is not your Savior.
She cannot heal every childhood wound.
She cannot satisfy every emotional hunger.
She cannot bear the weight of your entire identity.
She cannot replace the Lord Jesus Christ.
And when a man expects his wife to provide what only God can ultimately give, marriage becomes a burden neither spouse was designed to carry.
The Gospel frees husbands from demanding worshipful devotion from their wives because their deepest identity is found in Christ.
A husband can love without making his wife's approval his god.
He can repent without believing that admitting failure destroys his worth.
He can serve without keeping score.
He can seek reconciliation without controlling the outcome.
Because he is no longer trying to prove he is the center of the universe.
Jesus is.
Now return to Ephesians 5.
Paul does not stop at verse 25.
He continues by describing Christ's purpose in giving Himself for the church: to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word, and ultimately to present her in splendor.
This is first and foremost about the saving and sanctifying work of Jesus, not about a husband's power to spiritually cleanse his wife.
Only Christ is the Savior of the church.
A husband cannot take Jesus' place.
But a husband's love should reflect the Savior's holy, self-giving concern for the good of His people.
That means he should care about his wife's spiritual flourishing.
Not merely whether she fulfills his expectations.
Not merely whether she keeps up appearances.
But whether she is being encouraged to know Christ, love His Word, exercise her God-given gifts, and grow in grace.
And a spiritually mature husband does not confuse spiritual care with spiritual control.
He does not use prayer to manipulate.
He does not quote Bible verses as weapons.
He does not demand obedience to sinful behavior and call it submission.
He does not prevent his wife from seeking wise counsel.
He remembers that she belongs ultimately to Jesus Christ, not to him.
And in Ephesians 5:28–29, Paul adds another astonishing dimension.
Husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies.
No one normally hates his own flesh, Paul says, but nourishes and cherishes it.
The Greek verbs ἐκτρέφει (ektrephei) and θάλπει (thalpei) communicate nourishing and cherishing care.
This is not permission for possessiveness.
It is a call to attentive, protective, life-giving love within the profound unity of marriage.
A husband should not look at his wife's exhaustion and think, "Why isn't she doing more for me?"
He should be capable of asking, "How can I help carry what is overwhelming her?"
He should notice when she is hurting.
He should make room for her thoughts.
He should recognize that her dreams, grief, spiritual struggles, physical limitations, and emotional needs matter.
And when she speaks, he should remember that listening is not surrendering his dignity.
Sometimes the most loving thing a husband can do is put down his phone.
Turn off the television.
Stop preparing his defense.
Look into his wife's eyes.
And listen.
Not to win.
Not to correct every detail.
Not to prove that his suffering is greater.
But because the woman speaking is someone he promised to love.
Of course, Christian marriage is not built upon the assumption that wives are always right and husbands are always wrong.
Both spouses are sinners in need of grace.
Both are called to love, forgiveness, truthfulness, and faithfulness.
Ephesians 5:21 calls believers to submit to one another in the fear of Christ, immediately before Paul's household instructions.

Christians differ in how they understand the specific roles described in the verses that follow, but no faithful reading can turn a husband's command to love sacrificially into permission for cruelty or selfish domination.
And neither spouse is called to excuse sin.
Love is not the abandonment of truth.
Love tells the truth with humility.
Love establishes appropriate boundaries.
Love pursues peace without pretending that evil is good.
Love does not rejoice in wrongdoing.
As 1 Corinthians 13:6 says, it "rejoiceth in the truth."
And that brings us to the part many men would rather avoid.
You may be respected at church.
You may be admired at work.
You may have people who call you a good man.
But what happens when the door closes?
When there is no audience?
When nobody is applauding your generosity?
When your wife disagrees with you?
When she needs tenderness and you would rather withdraw?
When she points out something painful and your pride begins looking for an escape?
Who are you then?
Because public reputation and private character are not always the same thing.
And the Lord who sees what is done in secret is not deceived by appearances.
Brother, imagine something for a moment.
Imagine reaching the final years of your life.
The children are grown.
The career is behind you.
The house is quieter than it has ever been.
And you look across the room at the woman who has walked through decades with you.
She has seen you at your strongest.
And at your weakest.
She has witnessed your failures, disappointments, fears, and victories.
Her face carries the marks of passing years.
Your own hands are no longer as steady as they once were.
And in that quiet room, the question is no longer how much money you earned.
Or how impressive your title became.
Or how many people admired you.
The question is whether the woman beside you experienced your love as a faithful reflection of Christ.
Did you learn to cherish her?
Did you repent when you wounded her?
Did you become more gentle with age?
Did you make it easier for her to speak honestly?
Did you pray with her and for her?
Did you treat her dignity as precious?
Did you walk with her through suffering rather than abandoning her emotionally?
Did you love her when life became ordinary?
Because a marriage is not built only in dramatic moments.
It is shaped through thousands of ordinary decisions.
A gentle answer.
An honest apology.
A difficult conversation.
A promise kept.
A temptation resisted.
A burden shared.
A prayer whispered together when neither person knows what tomorrow will bring.
And yes, sometimes through counseling, pastoral care, and the courage to seek help before a relationship breaks further.
The spectacular moments may become memories.
But the ordinary patterns become the atmosphere of a home.
And that atmosphere matters.
Especially to children watching what marriage looks like.
A son may learn something about manhood from how his father speaks to his mother.
A daughter may learn something about love from whether her father treats her mother with honor.
These influences are not destiny, and families can heal from painful examples.
But the example you set is not insignificant.
Your children do not need to see a perfect father.
They need to see a father who knows what to do when he sins.
A father who repents.
A father who asks forgiveness.
A father who takes responsibility.
A father who does not hide behind religion to escape accountability.
A father who shows them that following Jesus changes how a man behaves at home.
And perhaps you are reading this with a heavy heart.
Because you recognize yourself.
You remember the harsh words.
The anniversaries you neglected.
The promises you broke.
The nights you turned away when your wife needed you.
The moments when you cared more about winning an argument than protecting the relationship.
Perhaps there has even been betrayal.
And now the distance between you feels enormous.
Listen carefully.
Your sin may be serious, but it is not greater than the power of Jesus Christ to forgive a truly repentant sinner.
That does not guarantee your marriage will be restored.
It does not remove the consequences of your choices.
It does not entitle you to immediate trust or reconciliation.
But it means your failures do not have to be the final word about who you become.
This is why the Gospel is more than moral advice.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired ourselves.
Not after we had demonstrated perfect devotion.
Not after we had become worthy of the cross.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
That is grace.
And when grace truly captures a man's heart, it does not teach him to take sin lightly.
It teaches him to hate the sin that wounded his Savior and harmed the people he was called to love.
The cross both humbles us and gives us hope.
It exposes the ugliness of selfishness.
And it reveals the immeasurable mercy of God.
It tells the proud husband, "You need repentance."
It tells the ashamed husband, "You may come to Christ."
It tells the despairing husband, "Your past need not dictate every choice you make tomorrow."
And it tells every husband that the deepest answer to his marriage is not becoming the hero of his own story.
It is surrendering to the only true Savior.
Jesus Christ.
The One who loved His church and gave Himself for her.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One who grants forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in faith.
Brother, don't finish this article merely thinking, "That was powerful."
Do something with the truth.
If you need to apologize, apologize.
If you need to confess sin, stop hiding.
If your anger has frightened your family, seek qualified help and accountability.
If you have neglected your wife emotionally, begin learning to listen.
If your marriage is suffering, seek wise, trustworthy support rather than allowing pride to keep you isolated.
If you have been using Scripture to justify controlling behavior, repent and learn to read the Word under the lordship of the Christ who came to serve.
And if your wife has been faithfully loving you through difficult seasons, do not wait until a funeral, a hospital room, or a crisis to tell her what she means to you.
Tell her while she can hear you.
Honor her while you have the opportunity.
Pray for her today.
And remember that genuine change is measured over time, not by how emotional you become after reading one article.
Maybe tonight you will sit beside your wife and say something you should have said years ago.

"I know I've provided for this family. But I also know there have been times when I failed to love you well. I want to hear where I've hurt you. I want to grow. And I want my life to reflect Jesus more faithfully."
Then give her the freedom to respond honestly.
She may cry.
She may be cautious.
She may not be ready to believe you.
Listen anyway.
And let tomorrow's actions begin to confirm today's words.
Because the goal is not to make a beautiful speech.
The goal is to become a faithful man.
Not through your own righteousness.
But through the grace of God working in a surrendered life.
And to every wife reading this who has been wounded by the misuse of these verses: the command for your husband to love you like Christ does not mean you must silently endure mistreatment.
Your dignity matters to God.
Your safety matters.
You are not responsible for making another person repent.
And seeking help does not make you faithless.
The Jesus who calls husbands to sacrificial love is also the Lord who cares for the oppressed, the weary, and the brokenhearted.
His Word is not a weapon meant to keep you trapped in fear.
It is truth that calls sinners to repentance and offers hope to those who trust Him.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because grace erases accountability.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem lives that sin has devastated.
He can confront what is hidden.
He can humble what is proud.
He can heal what is wounded.
He can teach a selfish man to serve.
He can teach a hardened heart to repent.
And where reconciliation is possible and safe, He can give people the grace to pursue it with truth, patience, and integrity.
Maybe this article reached you at the exact moment you needed to hear these words.
Not to entertain you.
Not to flatter you.
But to remind you that your marriage, your character, and your walk with Jesus are too important to leave untouched by Scripture.
If you're a husband, what is one thing God is convicting you to change in the way you love your wife?
You don't have to expose private details or betray your spouse's confidence.
But you can write, "Lord, teach me to love like Christ."
Or perhaps, "Jesus, forgive me. I'm ready to change."
If you're fighting to become a more faithful husband, comment, "I'm still fighting for a Christ-centered marriage."
And if you're carrying pain that words cannot easily explain, you can simply comment, "Pray for me."
Let the comments become a place of prayer, encouragement, testimony, and biblical truth—not a place where people are shamed for their struggles.
Somebody else may find the courage to repent because you were willing to acknowledge your need for grace.
And please, don't keep this message to yourself.
You never know which husband is one honest encounter with Scripture away from confronting years of selfishness.
You never know which struggling couple needs to remember that Jesus still calls people toward repentance, truth, and hope.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter Scripture, face difficult truths, discover the grace of Jesus Christ, and grow in genuine discipleship.
These resources are meant to help you move beyond a moment of inspiration into a lifetime of learning, prayer, repentance, and spiritual maturity.
Not out of guilt.
Not because you must pay to receive God's favor.
But because sharing in the work of spreading biblical truth can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity.

Scripture teaches that believers may support Gospel ministry willingly and cheerfully. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
It is not a required biblical tithe, a purchase of spiritual blessings, or a measure of how much you love God.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation. The greater purpose is the ministry of God's Word.
Every sincere act of support matters.
Because this mission has never been about building an audience for the sake of numbers.
It is about pointing people to the Savior.
A husband learning to repent.
A wife discovering that God has not forgotten her.
A family beginning to seek healing.
A wandering believer returning to Scripture.
A sinner realizing that forgiveness is found in Jesus Christ.
And a community growing together in truth and grace.
That is worth laboring for.
That is worth praying for.
And for those who freely choose to support it, that is worth investing in.
But before you leave, return with me to the question that started everything.
What does "Husbands, love your wives" actually demand from men?
It demands more than provision.
More than affection.
More than religious appearances.
It calls husbands to a life of faithful, sacrificial, tender, truthful, repentant love that reflects Jesus Christ.
Not perfectly.
No husband can match the sinless Savior.
But sincerely.
Dependently.
Continually.
By the grace of God.
And perhaps the most important question tonight is not whether your wife knows you are a Christian.
It is whether she can see the character of Christ becoming more evident in the way you treat her.
Brother, the cross is not merely something you wear around your neck, display in your home, or mention in your prayers.
It is where the Savior gave Himself for His people.
And it is the pattern Paul places before husbands when he commands them to love.
So when you go home tonight, don't merely ask God to change your marriage.
Ask Him to change you.

Because one day, when the noise of this world has faded and all the things you worked so hard to accumulate are left behind, you will not regret having loved your wife with greater tenderness, humility, and faithfulness.
You will not regret the apology that humbled your pride.
You will not regret the time you gave her.
You will not regret the prayers you prayed together.
You will not regret the selfish habits you surrendered to Christ.
And you will never regret becoming more like the Savior who loved you first.
Don't wait until the woman beside you becomes a memory to become the man you promised to be.
